## Where This Fits
This week fills the hole W3 left open — **attention addresses by content and does not know where anything is** (W3 p42: permutation-equivariant without a mask; with a causal mask, position can only be inferred indirectly from the mask, Haviv et al. 2022) — and then asks at once how the fix breaks. Three parts: **where explicit position is added** (the inductive biases of learned absolute, sinusoidal, ALiBi, RoPE and NoPE; the RoPE derivation on the board is the one full derivation of the week), **how it breaks past the training length** (the phase argument → position interpolation → NTK-aware scaling → YaRN; the `rope_scaling` block in Llama 3.1's `config.json` is this line as it shipped), and **the gap between nominal and effective length** (lost in the middle, why needle-in-a-haystack is not enough, RULER- and NoLiMa-style evaluation). The message: **"can take 128k tokens" and "can use 128k tokens" are two different things, and a third — "what it costs to take them in" — is the ledger row we fill this week**: past $L \approx 12d$ the $L^2$ term of prefill overtakes the weight side, and the prefill throughput W3's demo 2 measured fell more than fivefold from 1k to 128k for exactly this reason. The last cost segment gives only the budget view of sparse attention (which term it attacks, why it must be trainable); the mechanisms belong to W6 (replacing what produces the KV) and W11 (serving). This week is the premise of W12 (does RAG still have a job). **The numerical check of RoPE is written live by the instructor** (demo 1); the extrapolation and lost-in-the-middle experiments are rehearsed in advance and replayed in class with two or three live queries. You do not need to run anything.

## Learning Objectives
1. Restate W3 p42 on the board (permutation-equivariant without a mask; with a causal mask, position is inferred only from the mask) and **compare the inductive biases of five ways to add position explicitly** — learned absolute (a lookup table, undefined beyond the table), sinusoidal (a fixed function that extrapolates in principle, though the model need not use it), ALiBi (a distance-proportional penalty on the logits: the most robust extrapolation, the least expressive), RoPE (a rotation, with relativity delivered by the dot product), NoPE (the mask alone) — and say how each one breaks at lengths it never saw.
2. Derive the relativity of RoPE: pair the $d_{\text{head}}$ coordinates of $\mathbf{q}_m, \mathbf{k}_n$ into $d_{\text{head}}/2$ complex numbers, use $\mathbf{R}_m^\top \mathbf{R}_n = \mathbf{R}_{n-m}$ to show that $(\mathbf{R}_m\mathbf{q}_m)^\top(\mathbf{R}_n\mathbf{k}_n)$ **depends only on $m - n$**; and state precisely that this relativity lives in the $\mathbf{q}^\top\mathbf{k}$ term alone — $\mathbf{V}$ is not rotated and the causal mask still carries absolute position — which is why the KV cache still holds (W3 p15) and why MLA's low-rank absorption does not commute with it (W3 p29).
3. Explain, with the wavelength $\lambda_i = 2\pi/\theta_i$, why extrapolation fails: the low-frequency dimensions that never complete a cycle within the training length $L_{\text{train}}$ enter **unseen phases** at longer positions; from this, say what position interpolation (every dimension divided by $s$), NTK-aware scaling (change the base $b$: high frequencies almost untouched, the lowest scaled by $s$) and YaRN (split by how many rotations a dimension completes within the training length: many → untouched, fewer than one → interpolated, a smooth ramp between, plus an attention temperature) each repair and what each costs — and **read off from Llama 3.1's `rope_scaling` block which of these it ships**.
4. Explain the attention sink as a structural consequence of softmax normalisation (W3 p40), and from it why StreamingLLM stays stable on streams far longer than the training length merely by keeping the KV of the first few tokens under a sliding window — and why this is **not** long-context ability: whatever left the window is gone.
5. State the design of the lost-in-the-middle experiment (the same answer placed at the beginning, middle and end of the context, distractors elsewhere, accuracy plotted against position), explain why needle-in-a-haystack is only a **lower-bound check** (exact string, single fact, no distractors), and say what RULER- and NoLiMa-style evaluations add (several needles, aggregation, variable tracking, no literal match).
6. Use the two ledger formulas to compute the three costs of long context — the $2\,n_{\text{layer}} L^2 d$ term of prefill overtaking $2NL$ once $L > 12d$, the $4\,n_{\text{layer}} L d$ of decode, and $M_{\text{KV}} \propto L$ — fill in the numbers for a real `config.json`, and state the budget view of sparse attention: letting each query read $k$ keys replaces $L$ by $k$, and **the real question is how those $k$ are chosen and whether the choice is trainable** (NSA's "natively trainable"; DSA in DeepSeek-V3.2 is the shipped version); mechanisms are left to W6 and W11.

## Demos
The programs for this week's demos, published as they are built. **You are not required to run anything** — the numbers on the slides are the rehearsal records checked in with the code — but the code is published so that you can read it, re-run it, and change it. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slide | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Demo 1 · RoPE's relativity, checked to float64](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w05_d1_rope_check) | p18, p19 | Three functions written from zero — $\theta_i$, the pairwise rotation $\mathbf{R}_m$, and the score $(\mathbf{R}_m\mathbf{q})^\top(\mathbf{R}_n\mathbf{k})$ — and three tests: the score is invariant under a shift of $m$ with $m - n$ fixed, to float64 rounding; the *additive* sinusoidal stamp under the same shift is not, and all of the motion sits in its cross terms; rotating $\mathbf{v}$ as well rotates the whole output by the absolute position. `wavelengths.py` prints the wavelength of each of the 64 pairs against two training lengths and two bases, the table behind p19 | `torch` only, CPU, float64 (`wavelengths.py`: standard library) | any laptop |
| [Demo 2 · Length extrapolation on last week's tiny GPT](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w05_d2_extrapolation) | p24 | W4 demo 1's character-level GPT (NoPE, trained at $L = 256$) retrained twice from the same initialisation — as it was, and with RoPE ($b = 10^4$) on $\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}$ — then run on held-out windows of 256, 512 and 1024 characters, recording the loss at every position; the RoPE model is then run again **without retraining** with position interpolation ($s = 4$) and with NTK-aware base scaling. Four per-position curves and the two-row table on the slide; everything is rehearsed beforehand and replayed in class | `torch` only; training on `mps` (≈ 20 min for both models), `replay` needs nothing | Apple silicon as tested; any machine with `torch` for `replay` |
| [Demo 3 · Lost in the middle, scaled down](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w05_d3_lost_in_middle) | p29 | The synthetic key–value retrieval of Liu et al. §4 on the Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (4-bit MLX) that W3 demo 2 measured: $K$ random UUID pairs as one JSON object, the answer pair moved to position $1, \lfloor K/4 \rfloor, \lfloor K/2 \rfloor, \lfloor 3K/4 \rfloor, K$ with everything else fixed, $Q = 20$ questions per position, two context sizes of about 4k and 16k tokens ($K$ calibrated to the token count). Exact-match accuracy per position — the table on the slide — and, for every wrong answer, what it was (another pair's value, a key, a UUID not in the context, none). Three questions are asked live in class; the rest is rehearsed and replayed | `mlx` + `mlx-lm`, the 4-bit model (≈ 4.5 GB) + 2 GiB of KV cache at 16k | **Apple silicon only** |

Demo 3's rehearsal record is not yet checked in; its table on the slide is filled once it is. Demo 4 (the StreamingLLM sink comparison) is added here when it is built. Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 27.0, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. "Any laptop" means the code depends on nothing platform-specific, not that it was verified elsewhere. Terminal prompts are in Chinese.

## References
- **JM3** ch 7 *Transformers and Pretraining* (the positional-encoding section; 2026-08-19 release); **RAS** ch 2, the closing section on positional embeddings (GPT-2-style learned absolute positions, the hand-written counterpart); **UDL** ch 12, the positional-encoding subsection
- Su et al., **RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding**, arXiv:2104.09864 (2021; v5 2023) — the original source of RoPE; the complex-number derivation in §3 is the one on the board this week
- Shaw, Uszkoreit & Vaswani, **Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations**, NAACL 2018 (arXiv:1803.02155) — the start of learned relative position embeddings; the first paper on the relative-bias line
- Press, Smith & Lewis, **Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation**, arXiv:2108.12409 (2021; v2 2022) — ALiBi; the abstract: trained at 1024, matches sinusoidal perplexity at 2048
- Haviv et al., **Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information**, Findings of EMNLP 2022 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2022.findings-emnlp.99) — cited in W3; recalled in this week's opening
- Kazemnejad et al., **The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.19466) — NoPE matches or beats explicit encodings on length generalisation in small-scale reasoning tasks (abstract); the hypothesis demo 2 tests
- Barbero et al., **Round and Round We Go! What makes Rotary Positional Encodings useful?**, arXiv:2410.06205 (2024; v3 2025) — on Gemma 7B, high frequencies carry position and low frequencies carry semantics (abstract); empirical support for the multi-resolution picture
- Chen et al., **Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation**, arXiv:2306.15595 (2023) — position interpolation; the abstract: LLaMA extended to 32k with minimal fine-tuning
- bloc97, **NTK-Aware Scaled RoPE allows LLaMA models to have extended (8k+) context size without any fine-tuning**, r/LocalLLaMA, June 2023 — **a Reddit forum post, not a paper**; the source of NTK-aware base scaling, listed in YaRN's references
- Peng et al., **YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models**, arXiv:2309.00071 (2023; v3 February 2026) — banded interpolation plus an attention temperature; the abstract claims ten times fewer tokens and 2.5 times fewer steps than earlier methods. **v3 is a major revision from February 2026**: re-read before quoting numbers
- Men et al., **Base of RoPE Bounds Context Length**, arXiv:2405.14591 (2024) — the base $b$ puts a lower bound on the reachable context length; too small a base yields only superficial long-context ability (abstract)
- Liu et al., **Scaling Laws of RoPE-based Extrapolation**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.05209) — a periodic view linking the extrapolation limit to $b$ and the fine-tuning length
- Grattafiori et al., **The Llama 3 Herd of Models**, arXiv:2407.21783 (2024) — the shipping record of Llama 3.1's 128k and its `rope_scaling`; the RoPE base and staged extension are in §3.4 (**body, not abstract**)
- Xiao et al., **Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2309.17453) — StreamingLLM; where W3's sink is put to use
- Gu et al., **When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View**, ICLR 2025 (Spotlight) (arXiv:2410.10781) — sinks come from softmax normalisation; with sigmoid attention they do not appear (abstract, models up to 1B)
- Liu et al., **Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts**, TACL 12 (2024), 157–173 (arXiv:2307.03172; DOI 10.1162/tacl_a_00638) — **the week's central critical paper**; the synthetic key-value retrieval of §4 is the design of demo 3
- Kamradt, **Needle In A Haystack — pressure testing LLMs**, GitHub `gkamradt/LLMTest_NeedleInAHaystack`, November 2023 — **a code repository, not a paper**; where the name NIAH comes from
- Hong, Troynikov & Huber, **Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance**, Chroma technical report, July 2025 — **a company technical report, not peer-reviewed**; across 18 models, longer inputs make performance less reliable
- Hsieh et al., **RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?**, COLM 2024 (arXiv:2404.06654) — extends NIAH with several needles, multi-hop tracing and aggregation; the abstract: most models degrade sharply with length, only about half hold up at 32k
- Modarressi et al., **NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching**, ICML 2025 (PMLR 267:44554–44570; arXiv:2502.05167) — needles with almost no lexical overlap with the question, so the model must associate; the abstract: 13 models drop sharply with length, and chain-of-thought does not close the gap
- Yen et al., **HELMET: How to Evaluate Long-Context Language Models Effectively and Thoroughly**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2410.02694) — the abstract: across 59 models, NIAH scores **do not predict** downstream performance; seven application-centric categories up to 128k
- Zhang et al., **∞Bench: Extending Long Context Evaluation Beyond 100K Tokens**, arXiv:2402.13718 (2024) — average length above 100k, English and Chinese, designed so that passage retrieval alone is not enough
- Bai et al., **LongBench v2: Towards Deeper Understanding and Reasoning on Realistic Long-context Multitasks**, arXiv:2412.15204 (2024) — 503 questions over 8k–2M words; the abstract: human experts score 53.7% under a time limit, the best direct-answer model 50.1% — long-context tasks call for reasoning and inference-time compute (a hook for W10)
- Xiong et al., **Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models**, arXiv:2309.16039 (2023) — continued pre-training of Llama 2 on long sequences; **the change to the RoPE base is in the body — the abstract only says it "discusses the limitation" of Llama's position encoding on long dependencies**
- Ding et al., **LongRoPE: Extending LLM Context Window Beyond 2 Million Tokens**, arXiv:2402.13753 (2024) — searches the non-uniformities of interpolation, extends progressively, then readjusts on short context; the cost "readjust short context afterwards" is stated in the abstract
- Li et al., **Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach**, EMNLP 2024 industry track (arXiv:2407.16833) — Self-Route; planted here, developed in W12
- Yuan et al., **Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention**, ACL 2025 best paper (arXiv:2502.11089; Anthology 2025.acl-long.1126) — **the point is "natively trainable", not inference-only**
- DeepSeek-AI, **DeepSeek-V3.2: Pushing the Frontier of Open Large Language Models**, arXiv:2512.02556 (2025) — DSA is the first contribution listed in the abstract; sparse attention as shipped
- Lu et al., **MoBA: Mixture of Block Attention for Long-Context LLMs**, arXiv:2502.13189 (2025) — another trainable block-selection route (preprint)
- Zhang et al., **H₂O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2306.14048) — the representative KV-eviction method; returns in W11
- Meta AI, **The Llama 4 herd**, April 2025 blog post — **a blog post, not a paper** (Llama 4 has no technical report); iRoPE: most layers RoPE, a few interleaved layers with no positional encoding
- Million-token context as shipped in 2026 (DeepSeek-V4's 1M, Qwen2.5-1M's DCA): search *Qwen2.5-1M technical report dual chunk attention*, *DeepSeek-V4 million-token context*; examples of nominal length, no scores quoted
